narrative:
The model estimated a 56.7% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt—slightly more likely than not—and that estimate is why your application was denied. This is not a certainty; it means the available information placed you just on the failure side of the admission decision.

The strongest reason was your third-year class-rank decile: you were in the second decile, well below the accepted-student average of about the sixth decile. That was the single most influential factor and it pushed the prediction toward bar failure. Your LSAT score of 39 was the next most important factor, but it worked in your favor: it was above the accepted average of about 37 and pushed toward passing. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.10 was the third most important factor and, in the model’s overall assessment, also modestly favored passing, even though it was slightly below the accepted average of 3.23. So the denial was driven mainly by your low third-year rank, not by your LSAT or GPA.

Next, ask admissions for an individualized review and explain any context behind your third-year performance, such as illness, work demands, or an upward trend. Ask whether additional coursework, a delayed start, or supporting letters could address the third-year concern. Emphasize that your LSAT and GPA were not the reason for denial, and request clarity on what evidence would change the decision.
